short: How many times per second a screen redraws the picture. Higher numbers make scrolling, games and motion look smoother.
body: Refresh rate is measured in hertz (Hz): a 60 Hz screen shows up to 60 new images per second, a 120 Hz screen up to 120. The difference is easiest to see when scrolling a web page or playing a fast game.
Many phones and laptops use an adaptive (variable) refresh rate. They drop to 1–10 Hz when the image is still to save battery and jump to 120 Hz or more when you scroll.

A high refresh rate only helps if the content keeps up. Films are mostly 24 frames per second, so for TV watching the panel quality matters more than 120 or 144 Hz. For gaming, the console or graphics card must produce enough frames to use it.
good: In 2026, 120 Hz is standard on mid-range and flagship phones and tablets; 60 Hz is now budget territory. Gaming monitors start around 144–180 Hz, with 240 Hz and higher for competitive players; good TVs offer 120 Hz (some 144 Hz).

short: How bright a screen can get, measured in nits (candela per square metre). Matters most outdoors and for HDR video.
body: One nit is the light of roughly one candle spread over a square metre. Indoors, 300–500 nits is comfortable; in direct sunlight a phone needs well over 1,000 nits to stay readable.

Spec sheets often quote peak brightness, which a screen may reach only on a small part of the picture for a few seconds, usually during HDR content. Full-screen, sustained brightness is lower, sometimes much lower.
Brands measure in different ways, so compare numbers with care. Independent reviews that measure full-screen and 10% window brightness give a fairer picture.
good: Flagship phones in 2026 advertise peak figures of 2,000–4,000+ nits; 1,000+ nits sustained outdoors is good. Laptops are fine at 400–500 nits, while HDR monitors and TVs benefit from 1,000 nits or more.

short: A screen type where every pixel makes its own light and can switch fully off, giving perfect blacks and very high contrast.
body: OLED stands for organic light-emitting diode. Unlike LCD screens, there is no backlight: each pixel glows on its own. A black pixel is simply switched off, so dark scenes look deep and there is no grey glow around bright objects.
OLED panels also react almost instantly, which keeps motion sharp, and they can be very thin or even foldable.

The trade-offs: full-screen brightness is usually lower than the best LCDs, prices are higher, and static elements shown for many hours (news tickers, taskbars) can cause permanent burn-in. Modern panels use pixel shifting and refresh routines to reduce this risk.
good: OLED is now the norm on mid-range and flagship phones and on smartwatches, and common on premium TVs, laptops and gaming monitors in 2026.

short: Active-matrix OLED: the OLED technology used in most phones and watches. Each pixel lights itself and blacks are truly black.
body: AMOLED means active-matrix organic light-emitting diode. The active matrix is the thin-film transistor layer that switches each pixel on and off quickly. In practice, AMOLED is simply the name most phone makers use for their OLED screens.

Names like Super AMOLED, Dynamic AMOLED or LTPO AMOLED are brand or feature labels on top of the same basic technology. LTPO is worth noting: it lets the screen lower its refresh rate down to around 1 Hz to save battery.
Benefits and drawbacks are the same as OLED: excellent contrast and fast response, with some risk of burn-in from static images over long periods.
good: Almost every phone above the entry level uses an AMOLED/OLED screen in 2026; LTPO with 1–120 Hz adaptive refresh is typical on flagships.

short: An LCD screen with thousands of tiny LEDs behind it, split into dimming zones for brighter HDR and deeper blacks than ordinary LCD.
body: Mini-LED is still an LCD: the pixels themselves do not light up. Behind them sits a backlight made of thousands of very small LEDs grouped into local dimming zones that can brighten or dim separately.
More zones generally means better control. A screen with a few hundred zones handles dark scenes far better than a standard LCD, while models with thousands of zones come close to OLED-like contrast.

Mini-LED can get very bright, which suits HDR and sunny rooms, and it has no burn-in risk. The weakness is blooming: a faint halo around bright objects on a dark background, because a zone is much bigger than a single pixel.
good: In 2026 Mini-LED is common in mid-range and premium TVs, some monitors, tablets and laptops. Look for the number of dimming zones and real-world reviews of blooming.

short: A type of LCD known for accurate colours and wide viewing angles. Common in monitors, laptops and budget phones.
body: IPS (in-plane switching) is one of the main LCD technologies. Its liquid crystals move sideways, so colours and brightness stay consistent even when you look at the screen from an angle.
IPS panels are popular for office work, photo editing and general use because colours look natural. Modern fast IPS panels are also good for gaming.
The main weakness is contrast: typical IPS screens reach about 1,000:1, so blacks look dark grey in a dim room. Some show IPS glow, a faint light at the corners on dark images.
good: IPS remains the default for affordable and mid-range monitors and laptops in 2026; fast IPS gaming monitors commonly reach 180–240 Hz.

short: An LCD type with much deeper blacks than IPS, good for films and dark rooms, but with narrower viewing angles.
body: VA stands for vertical alignment. Its liquid crystals block the backlight better than IPS, so contrast is usually around 3,000:1 to 5,000:1, about three to five times higher. Dark scenes look noticeably deeper.
Many TVs and curved monitors use VA panels. They are a good choice for films and games in a dim room.
Downsides: colours and contrast shift when you look from the side, and cheaper VA panels can show dark smearing, where dark objects leave short trails during fast motion.
good: VA is common in budget and mid-range TVs and curved gaming monitors in 2026. Check reviews for dark-transition smearing if you play fast games.

short: Video and display technology that shows brighter highlights, deeper shadows and richer colours than standard (SDR) content.
body: HDR content carries extra information about brightness and colour. On a capable screen, sunlight reflections, fire or neon signs look bright and vivid while shadows keep their detail.

The main formats are HDR10 (the basic open standard), HDR10+ and Dolby Vision (both adjust the picture scene by scene), and HLG (used for broadcast TV). Most streaming services, game consoles and 4K Blu-rays offer HDR.

An HDR label alone does not guarantee a good result. A screen needs real brightness and contrast to show HDR well; a dim, low-contrast panel may accept HDR signals but look flat. For monitors, VESA DisplayHDR levels (400, 600, 1000, True Black) give a rough guide.
good: In 2026 nearly all 4K TVs support HDR10 and HLG. For a convincing effect, look for 1,000+ nits peak with local dimming or OLED; on monitors, DisplayHDR 600 or higher, or True Black for OLED.

short: An HDR format that adjusts brightness and colour scene by scene, supported by many streaming services and TVs.
body: Dolby Vision is a licensed HDR format. Like HDR10+, it uses dynamic metadata: the video tells the TV how to show each scene, rather than using one setting for the whole film.
Netflix, Disney+, Apple TV and many 4K Blu-rays offer Dolby Vision content, and many phones can record it. Xbox Series consoles also support it for games.

If a TV lacks Dolby Vision, the same content usually plays in HDR10 instead, so you still get HDR. The difference is noticeable mainly on mid-range screens, where scene-by-scene tuning helps the TV handle highlights it cannot fully reproduce.
good: Many brands support Dolby Vision in 2026; some support HDR10+ instead, and a few support both. Supporting both is the safest choice.

short: The number of pixels a screen shows, written as width × height. More pixels mean sharper detail at the same size.
body: Common labels: Full HD is 1920 × 1080 pixels, QHD (1440p) is 2560 × 1440, 4K UHD is 3840 × 2160 and 8K is 7680 × 4320. 4K has four times the pixels of Full HD.

Whether you see the difference depends on screen size and distance. On a 140 cm (55 in) TV seen from the sofa, 4K is clearly sharper than Full HD, while 8K adds little because there is very little 8K content.
Higher resolution also needs more power. For gaming monitors, a graphics card must work harder at 4K than at 1440p, which can lower frame rates.
good: 4K is standard for TVs from about 109 cm (43 in) up in 2026. For monitors, 1440p suits 68–69 cm (27 in) gaming screens, and 4K suits 68–81 cm (27–32 in) for work and sharp text.

short: Pixels per inch: how tightly pixels are packed. Higher PPI gives sharper text and images at the same viewing distance.
body: PPI counts how many pixels fit along one inch (2.54 cm) of screen. The same resolution looks sharper on a smaller screen because the pixels are packed more densely.
How much you need depends on distance. A phone held 30 cm away looks sharp from about 400 PPI; a monitor at arm's length looks crisp from roughly 110–160 PPI; a TV across the room needs far less.
Beyond a certain point the eye cannot see extra detail, so very high PPI mainly costs battery and performance. Compare PPI only between devices of the same type.
good: In 2026 most mid-range and flagship phones sit around 400–500 PPI. A 68 cm (27 in) 1440p monitor is about 109 PPI, a 68 cm (27 in) 4K monitor about 163 PPI.

short: How quickly a pixel changes colour, in milliseconds. Lower values mean less blur and fewer trails behind moving objects.
body: Response time measures how long a pixel needs to switch from one shade to another, usually grey-to-grey (GtG). If it is too slow, moving objects leave ghostly trails.

Manufacturer figures like 1 ms are often measured under ideal settings, sometimes with aggressive overdrive that causes overshoot, a bright halo around moving edges. Independent tests are more reliable.
OLED pixels switch in well under 1 ms, so motion looks very clean. Fast IPS panels are good, and VA panels can be slower, especially in dark scenes.
good: In 2026, gaming monitors around 1–5 ms real-world GtG are good; OLED monitors are near-instant. For office use, response time hardly matters.

short: The difference between the brightest white and the darkest black a screen can show. Higher ratios mean deeper, richer images.
body: A contrast ratio of 1,000:1 means white is 1,000 times brighter than black. The higher the number, the less greyish black looks, which matters most in dark rooms and dark scenes.
Typical values: IPS panels about 1,000:1, VA panels about 3,000–5,000:1. Mini-LED with local dimming goes much higher, and OLED has near-infinite contrast because its black pixels are fully off.
Be careful with dynamic contrast figures in the millions: they compare different moments of brightness rather than what you see at the same time. Native or static contrast is the meaningful number.
good: For monitors in 2026, 1,000:1 is acceptable, 3,000:1 or more is good for films and games; OLED or Mini-LED with many zones is best for dark content.

short: How much of a standard range of colours a screen can show. sRGB is the web standard; DCI-P3 is the wider one for HDR video.
body: A colour gamut is the range of colours a display can reproduce. sRGB is the standard for websites, most photos and Windows. DCI-P3 is wider and used for films, HDR content and Apple devices. Adobe RGB matters mainly for print work.

Coverage is shown as a percentage, for example 99% sRGB. Close to 100% sRGB means everyday content looks as intended. Covering much more than sRGB is useful for HDR, but without proper colour management it can make normal content look oversaturated.
Coverage is not the same as accuracy. A screen can cover a wide gamut yet show colours slightly off. Reviews often list Delta E; below 2 is very hard to tell apart from perfect.
good: In 2026, 95–100% sRGB is expected on decent monitors and laptops; creative and HDR screens should also reach about 90%+ DCI-P3.

short: Adaptive sync technologies that match the screen's refresh to the game's frame rate, removing tearing and reducing stutter.
body: When a graphics card's frame rate does not match the monitor's refresh rate, the image can tear (split horizontally) or stutter. Adaptive sync lets the screen wait for each new frame instead.

AMD FreeSync and NVIDIA G-Sync are the two main brands; both build on the open VESA Adaptive-Sync standard. Most monitors labelled G-Sync Compatible are FreeSync screens tested to work with NVIDIA cards, so in practice many monitors work with both.
Higher tiers such as FreeSync Premium add low framerate compensation, which keeps things smooth when frame rates drop low. On TVs, the HDMI 2.1 equivalent is VRR, which modern consoles use.
good: In 2026 virtually every gaming monitor supports adaptive sync. FreeSync Premium or G-Sync Compatible is a sensible minimum; for TVs, look for HDMI 2.1 VRR.

short: A monitor whose screen bends towards you, keeping the edges at a similar distance from your eyes. Most useful on wide screens.
body: Curvature is described by a radius in millimetres: 1000R means the curve would form a circle with a 1 m radius. A smaller number such as 800R means a stronger curve; 1800R is gentle.
On ultrawide monitors of 86 cm (34 in) and larger, a curve makes the edges easier to see without turning your head and adds immersion in games and simulators.
On smaller 16:9 screens the benefit is minor. Curves can also make straight lines look bent, which some designers and engineers dislike, and they can catch reflections from more directions.
good: In 2026 curves of 1500R–1800R are typical for ultrawide monitors, with 800R–1000R for very wide gaming screens. Flat panels remain the norm at 68 cm (27 in) and below.

short: The shape of a screen: width compared with height. 16:9 is standard; 21:9 ultrawide and 16:10 are popular alternatives.
body: 16:9 is the shape of most TVs, monitors and videos. 16:10 is slightly taller and common on laptops, giving more room for documents and web pages. 3:2 and 4:3 are taller still and used on some tablets and laptops.
Ultrawide monitors use 21:9 (for example 3440 × 1440), and super-ultrawide 32:9 is like two 16:9 screens side by side. They are great for multitasking, video editing and racing or flight games.
Content that does not match the screen shape shows black bars. Most films fill a 16:9 TV almost fully, but not all games support ultrawide formats.
good: In 2026, 16:10 is standard on most new laptops, 16:9 for most monitors and all TVs, and 21:9 a popular choice for monitors of 86 cm (34 in).

short: Milliampere-hours: how much charge a battery holds. A rough guide to battery life when comparing similar devices.
body: mAh measures the electric charge a battery can store. A 5,000 mAh phone battery holds more than a 4,000 mAh one, but real battery life also depends on the screen, processor and software, so a smaller battery can still last longer.

For power banks, the rated mAh is measured at the internal cell voltage (about 3.6–3.85 V). Some energy is lost when converting to USB voltage, so a 10,000 mAh power bank typically delivers around 60–70% of that capacity to your phone.
Newer silicon-carbon batteries store more energy in the same space, which is why many 2025–2026 phones have noticeably higher mAh figures without getting thicker.
good: In 2026, about 5,000 mAh is typical for Android phones and 6,000–7,000 mAh is increasingly common; smartwatches range from roughly 300 to 600 mAh.

short: Watt-hours measure the energy a battery stores. It is the fairest way to compare laptop batteries and air-travel limits.
body: Watt-hours combine charge and voltage, so they show real stored energy. That makes Wh more comparable than mAh between devices with different battery voltages, which is why laptops are rated in Wh.
As a rough guide, a laptop using 10 W on average would run about 6 hours on a 60 Wh battery. Actual battery life depends heavily on the screen, processor and what you are doing.
Airlines usually allow batteries up to 100 Wh in cabin baggage without approval; 100–160 Wh typically needs airline permission. Power banks must go in carry-on, not checked luggage.
good: In 2026, thin laptops typically have about 50–75 Wh; larger and gaming laptops often reach 80–99.9 Wh, just under the 100 Wh flight limit.

short: Charging that delivers more power than standard, filling a battery in a fraction of the time. Usually measured in watts.
body: Charging speed depends on power in watts (volts × amps). A basic USB charger gives 5–10 W; fast chargers for phones range from about 25 W to over 100 W.

Fast charging is quickest from empty up to about 50–80%, then slows to protect the battery. Both the device and the charger (and cable) must support the same standard, usually USB Power Delivery, or a brand's own system.

For headphones and earbuds, fast charging means a short charge gives hours of playback, for example 5–10 minutes giving one to a few hours of listening. Heat is the main enemy of battery lifespan, and many devices offer optimised charging to limit wear.
good: In 2026 phones commonly charge at 25–45 W, with some brands at 80–120 W. For earbuds, roughly 1 hour of playback from a 5–10 minute charge is a good result.

short: Charging by placing a device on a pad instead of plugging in a cable. Qi and Qi2 are the common standards.
body: Wireless charging uses magnetic induction between a coil in the pad and a coil in the device. Qi is the universal standard used by most phones, earbuds cases and some watches.

Qi2 adds magnets that snap the device into the right position, improving efficiency and allowing up to 15 W, with a newer 25 W version. Many smartwatches use their own magnetic chargers instead of standard Qi.
Wireless charging is convenient but slower and less efficient than a cable, and it produces more heat. For earbuds and watches, the main benefit is simply not needing a cable.
good: In 2026, Qi2 is supported by most new flagship phones; 15 W is common, 25 W on newer models. A wireless-charging case is a nice extra on mid-range and premium earbuds.

short: USB-C is the reversible connector now standard on most devices; USB Power Delivery (PD) is the charging standard that runs over it.
body: USB-C is just the shape of the plug. What it can do depends on the version: USB 2.0 transfers data at 480 Mbps, while USB 3.x, USB4 and Thunderbolt go from 5 to 40 Gbps or more and can carry video.

USB Power Delivery lets a charger and device agree on voltage and power. It covers everything from earbuds to laptops, up to 240 W with the newest cables. One good PD charger can charge many different devices.
In the EU, USB-C charging has been required for phones, tablets, earbuds and many other small devices since late 2024, and for laptops since April 2026.
good: In 2026, look for USB-C with PD on everything. A 65 W PD charger handles phones, tablets and most thin laptops; check whether a phone's port is USB 2.0 or faster if you move large files by cable.

short: The fifth generation of mobile networks, offering faster data and lower delays than 4G where coverage is available.
body: 5G speeds vary greatly. Most coverage uses mid-band frequencies, giving everyday speeds from tens to several hundred Mbps. Millimetre-wave 5G is much faster but works only over short distances and is rare outside a few countries.
Standalone 5G (5G SA) runs on a fully new core network and enables features like lower latency; many networks still use non-standalone 5G built on 4G infrastructure.
For a buyer, 5G support in a phone or tablet is useful for the future, but your real speed depends on your operator and location. Check that the device supports the 5G bands used in your country.
good: In 2026 almost every new phone above the entry level supports 5G. On tablets, 5G (cellular) versions cost extra and are only worth it if you need internet away from Wi-Fi.

short: Generations of Wi-Fi. Newer versions are faster and handle crowded networks better, but need a matching router to benefit.
body: Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax) improved speed and efficiency in homes with many devices. Wi-Fi 6E added the 6 GHz band, which is less crowded and good for short-range high speed. Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be) adds wider 320 MHz channels and Multi-Link Operation, which uses several bands at once for speed and stability.
Your connection is only as fast as the slowest link: device, router and internet plan. A Wi-Fi 7 laptop on a Wi-Fi 5 router behaves like Wi-Fi 5.
Walls and distance reduce speed far more than the Wi-Fi version does. A mesh system often helps more in a large home than a newer standard.
good: In 2026 Wi-Fi 6E or 7 is standard on flagship phones and most new laptops; Wi-Fi 6 is fine for TVs and mid-range devices.

short: The Bluetooth standard a device supports. Newer versions bring better range, efficiency and audio features.
body: Bluetooth 5.0 and later brought better range and lower power use. Bluetooth 5.2 introduced LE Audio, which uses the LC3 codec for good sound at lower power and enables Auracast, a way to share one audio stream with many headphones. Bluetooth 5.3, 5.4 and 6.0 add further refinements in reliability and location features.
Both devices must support a feature for it to work. Pairing Bluetooth 5.4 earbuds with an older phone still works, but only with the features both share.
The version number says little about sound quality on its own; codecs and the headphones themselves matter more.
good: In 2026, Bluetooth 5.3 or newer is typical on phones, laptops and headphones; LE Audio and Auracast support is a useful extra.

short: Near-field communication: short-range wireless used for contactless payments, transit cards and quick pairing.
body: NFC works only over a few centimetres, which makes it suitable for tapping to pay or entering public transport. On a smartwatch it lets you pay with Google Wallet, Apple Pay, Samsung Wallet or similar services without your phone.
Having NFC hardware does not guarantee payments work: the watch's software and your bank must support the payment service in your country.
NFC is also used to pair headphones or speakers with one tap and to read digital keys and ID tags.
good: In 2026 NFC is standard on nearly all phones and most mid-range and premium smartwatches; some budget fitness bands still skip it or offer it only in certain versions.

short: A digital SIM built into the device. You activate a mobile plan by scanning a code instead of inserting a plastic card.
body: An eSIM is a chip soldered inside the phone, tablet or watch that can store one or more operator profiles. You add a plan through a QR code or the operator's app.
eSIM makes it easy to switch operators, use two numbers on one phone, or buy a local data plan when travelling. Smartwatches with eSIM can make calls and use data without your phone nearby.
Some phones are now eSIM-only, so check that your operator supports eSIM before buying. Moving an eSIM to a new phone is usually done in settings or through the operator.
good: In 2026 eSIM is supported by almost all flagship and many mid-range phones in Europe; cellular smartwatches rely on eSIM.

short: The HDMI version that supports 4K at 120 Hz, variable refresh rate and other gaming features over one cable.
body: HDMI 2.1 raises bandwidth to up to 48 Gbps, enough for 4K at 120 Hz or 144 Hz with HDR. It also adds VRR (variable refresh rate) and ALLM (auto low latency mode), which modern consoles and PCs use for smoother, quicker gaming.
Not every HDMI 2.1 port has all features or full bandwidth, so check what the TV or monitor actually supports and how many ports have it. You also need an Ultra High Speed HDMI cable.
HDMI 2.2, announced in 2025, raises bandwidth to 96 Gbps, but devices with it are still rare. For most people HDMI 2.1 is what matters.
good: In 2026, a gaming TV should have at least two full HDMI 2.1 ports with 4K 120 Hz and VRR. On laptops, an HDMI 2.1 port allows 4K 120 Hz external displays.

short: Enhanced Audio Return Channel: an HDMI feature that sends full-quality sound from the TV to a soundbar or AV receiver.
body: With eARC, apps and devices connected to your TV can send their sound back down a single HDMI cable to a soundbar or receiver. You can control volume with the TV remote.
The older ARC carries only compressed surround sound. eARC has much more bandwidth, so it can pass lossless formats such as Dolby TrueHD and Dolby Atmos in its highest-quality form.
Both the TV port and the sound system must support eARC. It usually works on just one specific HDMI port on the TV, labelled ARC or eARC.
good: In 2026 eARC is standard on mid-range and premium TVs and soundbars. It is worth having if you plan to add a Dolby Atmos soundbar.

short: A video connection mainly used by PCs and monitors, supporting high resolutions and refresh rates.
body: DisplayPort is common on desktop graphics cards and monitors. DisplayPort 1.4 handles 4K at around 120–144 Hz using compression (DSC), and DisplayPort 2.1 offers up to 80 Gbps for very high resolutions and refresh rates.
Many laptops send DisplayPort signals through their USB-C or Thunderbolt ports (DisplayPort Alt Mode), so one cable can connect a monitor and sometimes charge the laptop too.
For PC gaming, DisplayPort usually gives the best support for high refresh rates and adaptive sync. Game consoles use HDMI instead.
good: In 2026, DisplayPort 1.4 with DSC is enough for most gaming monitors; DisplayPort 2.1 matters for 4K at 240 Hz and similar high-end setups.

short: An international code showing how well a device is protected against dust and water. IP68 is the highest common rating.
body: The IP code has two digits. The first (0–6) is dust protection: 6 means dust-tight. The second (0–9) is water: 4 means splashes, 7 means immersion up to 1 m for 30 minutes, 8 means deeper or longer immersion as specified by the manufacturer, often 1.5 m or more.
An X instead of a number (for example IPX4) means that part was not tested. IPX4 earbuds survive sweat and rain but not swimming.

Ratings are tested in fresh water in a lab. Salt water, chlorine, soap, hot water and pressure from jets can damage seals, and protection may weaken as a device ages. Most warranties do not cover water damage.
good: In 2026, IP68 is standard on flagship phones and many mid-range ones; IP54–IP57 is typical for sport earbuds; watches usually also list ATM ratings.

short: A watch rating in atmospheres that indicates water pressure resistance. 5 ATM suits swimming; it does not mean diving.
body: ATM ratings come from watch standards. 5 ATM means the watch withstands pressure equal to 50 m of still water in a lab, but in daily life it means it is suitable for swimming in a pool or the sea, not for diving.
10 ATM offers more margin for water sports. Diving needs a watch certified to a dive standard (such as ISO 6425), which only some rugged models have.
Movement in water, jumping in, hot showers, saunas and soap all add stress. Rinse a watch with fresh water after the sea or pool.
good: In 2026, most smartwatches and fitness bands are rated 5 ATM; rugged and sports models often offer 10 ATM, and a few are certified for recreational diving.

short: Toughened glass that protects screens from scratches and drops. Gorilla Glass is the best-known brand; others exist.
body: Most phones, tablets and watches use chemically strengthened glass over the display. Corning's Gorilla Glass, with versions like Victus and Armor, is the best-known; other makers include AGC (Dragontrail) and Schott, and some phones use in-house glass.

Newer generations generally improve drop resistance or scratch resistance, but there is always a trade-off between the two. No glass is unbreakable; how a phone lands matters more than the glass version.
Some watches use sapphire crystal, which is very scratch-resistant. A case and screen protector still offer the cheapest protection against costly repairs.
good: In 2026, flagship phones use the latest generation of toughened glass on the front, often on the back too; mid-range phones commonly use one or two generations older.

short: Cores and threads show how many tasks a CPU can work on at once; GHz shows how fast each one runs.
body: A core is a processing unit; threads are the tasks it can handle simultaneously. Many modern CPUs mix performance cores for heavy work with efficiency cores for light tasks and battery life, so total core counts are not directly comparable between brands.

Boost clock (GHz) is the top speed a core reaches for short periods. A higher boost helps quick, single-threaded tasks such as opening apps, while more cores help video editing, 3D rendering and compiling code.
GHz alone is not a fair comparison between generations or brands, because newer designs do more work per cycle. Benchmarks and reviews are a better guide.
good: In 2026, 8–12 threads are plenty for office and study laptops; 16 or more threads suit content creation and gaming. Boost clocks of about 4.5–5.5 GHz are typical on performance laptop chips.

short: Short-term working memory that holds open apps and data. More RAM lets a device keep more running smoothly at once.
body: RAM is separate from storage. It is fast but temporary: when it fills up, the device has to close background apps or swap data to slower storage, which feels like lag.

On phones, more RAM keeps apps and browser tabs open in the background and supports on-device AI features, which often need extra memory. On laptops, RAM matters for many browser tabs, large spreadsheets, photo editing and games.
In most thin laptops, tablets and phones, RAM is soldered and cannot be upgraded later, so it is worth buying enough at the start.
good: In 2026, phones: 8 GB minimum, 12–16 GB on flagships. Laptops: 16 GB is the sensible standard, 32 GB for creative work or heavy gaming. Tablets: 8 GB or more for multitasking.

short: Where apps, photos and files are kept permanently. UFS is used in phones and tablets, SSD in laptops.
body: Storage is measured in gigabytes (GB) or terabytes (TB). Part of it is used by the operating system, so a 128 GB phone gives you noticeably less free space.

Speed matters too. Phones use UFS storage; newer versions like UFS 4.0 load apps and save photos faster than UFS 3.1 or older eMMC. Laptops use SSDs, and NVMe SSDs are much faster than old hard drives or SATA SSDs.
Many phones no longer have microSD slots, and most thin laptops have only one SSD slot, so plan for your photos, videos and games before buying.
good: In 2026, phones: 256 GB is a comfortable base, 128 GB is tight. Laptops: 512 GB NVMe SSD minimum, 1 TB for gaming or video. Tablets: 128–256 GB for most people.

short: A separate graphics processor with its own memory, much faster than built-in graphics for games, 3D and video work.
body: Most laptops use integrated graphics built into the main processor. They are fine for browsing, video and light games, and recent integrated chips handle many older or less demanding games well.

A dedicated (discrete) GPU, such as NVIDIA GeForce RTX or AMD Radeon, has its own video memory (VRAM). It is needed for modern games at good settings, 3D modelling, and speeds up video editing and local AI tools.
The same GPU name can perform very differently between laptops depending on its power limit (in watts) and cooling. Dedicated GPUs also use more battery and add weight and heat.
good: In 2026, a gaming laptop should have at least an RTX 5050/5060-class GPU with 8 GB VRAM; for 1440p gaming or heavy creative work, more VRAM and a higher power limit help.

short: Headphones use microphones and anti-noise sound to reduce outside noise, especially low hums like engines and air conditioning.
body: ANC microphones listen to the noise around you, and the headphones play an opposite sound wave that cancels much of it. It works best on steady, low-frequency sound: aircraft cabins, buses and fans.
Sudden or high-pitched sounds such as voices or clattering are harder to cancel; a good fit and ear tips or cushions block those passively.

Many headphones also offer a transparency (ambient) mode that lets outside sound in, useful for traffic or conversations. ANC uses extra battery, and some people feel slight ear pressure with strong ANC.
good: In 2026 ANC is common even on mid-priced earbuds; premium over-ear models offer the strongest cancellation. Reviews with measured noise reduction are the best comparison.

short: The method used to compress audio sent over Bluetooth. Better codecs can improve sound quality or reduce delay.
body: SBC is the basic codec every device supports. AAC is used well by Apple devices. aptX variants (aptX Adaptive, aptX Lossless) are found on many Android phones with Qualcomm chips. LDAC, from Sony, allows higher bitrates, and LC3 is the newer LE Audio codec.
Both the phone and the headphones must support the same codec. iPhones use AAC and do not support aptX or LDAC.
In everyday listening, the fit and tuning of the headphones usually matter more than the codec. High-bitrate modes may also drop out more easily in crowded places.
good: In 2026, AAC plus either aptX Adaptive or LDAC is a good combination for Android users; iPhone users mostly need AAC. LC3 support is a useful bonus for the future.

short: The diameter of the speaker element inside headphones. Larger drivers can move more air, but size alone does not decide sound quality.
body: A driver is the tiny loudspeaker that makes sound. Earbuds typically use drivers of about 6–12 mm; over-ear headphones usually 30–50 mm.
Bigger drivers can produce bass more easily and play louder with less distortion, but tuning, materials, housing design and the fit on your ears matter just as much.
Some headphones use several drivers or different types, such as planar magnetic or balanced armature. Compare reviews and frequency measurements rather than relying on the millimetre figure alone.
good: In 2026, about 10–11 mm is common for earbuds and 40 mm for over-ear headphones; anything in these ranges can sound excellent if well tuned.

short: How much the headphones resist electrical current. High-impedance headphones may need an amplifier to sound loud enough.
body: Impedance is measured in ohms (Ω). Most wireless headphones and earbuds have built-in amplifiers, so impedance hardly matters for them.

For wired headphones, low impedance (around 16–32 Ω) works well with phones, laptops and dongles. High-impedance models (150–600 Ω) are mostly studio or audiophile headphones and often sound quiet without a headphone amplifier.
Sensitivity (dB per mW or per V) is the other half of the picture: it shows how loud headphones get from a given amount of power.
good: In 2026, under about 50 Ω is fine for phones and laptops without extra gear; above 150 Ω plan on a dedicated amplifier or DAC.

short: Lets headphones stay connected to two devices at once, such as a phone and a laptop, and switch between them automatically.
body: With multipoint, you can listen to music from your laptop and still take a call from your phone without re-pairing. The headphones usually switch to whichever device starts playing.

Most models connect to two devices at the same time; some remember more and let you choose in an app. Ecosystem features such as automatic switching between devices from one brand are a separate thing.
On some headphones, using multipoint disables the highest-quality codec, such as LDAC, or slightly reduces battery life.
good: In 2026 multipoint is standard on most mid-range and premium headphones and earbuds, and increasingly common on budget models.

short: The number of millions of pixels a camera sensor captures. More megapixels allow more cropping, but do not guarantee better photos.
body: A 50 MP camera captures 50 million pixels per photo. Many phones with 50 MP or higher sensors combine groups of pixels (pixel binning) to save 12–12.5 MP photos by default, which reduces noise in low light.
Photo quality depends more on sensor size, lens quality, aperture, stabilisation and image processing than on megapixels. A larger sensor collects more light, which matters most at night.
High megapixel counts help when cropping or zooming digitally, and for large prints.
good: In 2026, 50 MP main cameras are standard across mid-range and flagship phones; some use 200 MP sensors. Tablets are fine with 12–13 MP for documents and video calls.

short: The size of the lens opening that lets light in. A lower f-number means a wider opening and more light.
body: Aperture is written like f/1.8. Counter-intuitively, a smaller number means a bigger opening: f/1.6 lets in more light than f/2.2, which helps in dim scenes.
A wider aperture also creates a shallower depth of field, so the background looks softer. On phones, most of the blur in portrait mode comes from software, because the sensors are small.
Most phone lenses have a fixed aperture. Compare apertures only together with sensor size, since a large sensor at f/1.9 can gather more light than a small sensor at f/1.7.
good: In 2026, main phone cameras typically range from about f/1.4 to f/1.9; telephoto and ultra-wide lenses are usually narrower, around f/2.0–f/3.0 or beyond.

short: Zoom achieved with lenses rather than by cropping the image, keeping full detail at longer distances.
body: Phones get optical zoom from a separate telephoto camera. A 3x or 5x lens shows a distant subject larger without losing detail. Periscope designs fold the light sideways to fit longer zoom into a thin phone.

Digital zoom simply crops and enlarges the image, which loses detail quickly. Brands often advertise hybrid zoom such as 10x or 30x, combining a telephoto lens with cropping and processing; it can look good at moderate levels but gets soft at the extremes.
Look at the native optical zoom figure, such as 3x or 5x, and sample photos for a fair comparison.
good: In 2026, many flagships offer a 3x and/or 5x optical telephoto; mid-range phones increasingly include a 2–3x telephoto, while budget phones usually rely on digital zoom.

short: A mechanism that moves the lens or sensor to counter hand shake, giving sharper photos in low light and steadier video.
body: OIS uses tiny motors to shift the lens or sensor opposite to your hand movements. This lets the camera use slower shutter speeds in dim light without blurring.
Electronic stabilisation (EIS) works in software by cropping and shifting the video frame. It is effective for walking video but can reduce quality slightly. Many phones combine OIS and EIS.
OIS is especially valuable on telephoto cameras, because any shake is magnified when zoomed in.
good: In 2026, OIS on the main camera is common from the mid-range up; flagships typically add it on the telephoto too. Budget phones may have only EIS.

short: The EU's colour-coded label rating how efficiently an appliance or screen uses energy, from A (best) to G (worst).
body: Since 2021, TVs, monitors, fridges, washing machines and dishwashers use a rescaled A–G label, replacing the old A+++ scale. The new classes are strict on purpose, so a TV rated E or F today can be as efficient as one that was labelled A or A+ before.

For screens, the label shows separate classes for standard (SDR) and HDR viewing, plus power use in watts and kWh per 1,000 hours. HDR usually rates several classes worse because it needs more brightness.
Each label has a QR code linking to the EU EPREL database, where you can check the official figures.
good: In 2026, very few TVs reach class A or B for SDR; D–F is common, and G is typical for HDR mode. Monitors often score better because they are smaller.

short: How fast a washing machine drum spins at the end of the cycle, in revolutions per minute. Faster spinning leaves clothes drier.
body: Higher spin speeds remove more water, so clothes dry faster on a line or use less energy in a tumble dryer. The EU energy label shows a spin-drying efficiency class from A to G.
Typical washing machines spin at 1,200–1,600 rpm. The jump from 1,400 to 1,600 rpm removes a little more water but adds wear on fabrics and more creasing.
Most cycles for delicates, wool and synthetics use lower spin speeds anyway, so the maximum figure matters mainly for cottons and towels.
good: In 2026, 1,400 rpm is a sensible standard for most homes; 1,200 rpm is fine if you dry clothes outdoors, and 1,600 rpm helps if you use a tumble dryer often.

short: How loud an appliance is, in decibels. A lower number means quieter; every 10 dB higher sounds roughly twice as loud.
body: Decibels are logarithmic: 3 dB more means double the sound energy, and around 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud to most people. So 42 dB and 48 dB are noticeably different.

For reference, a quiet room is about 30 dB, normal conversation around 60 dB. Dishwashers and washing machines list noise in dB(A), which is weighted to match human hearing, and the EU label adds a noise class from A to D.
Washing machines are loudest when spinning, so check the spin noise figure, not only the washing figure, if the machine is near a bedroom or living area.
good: In 2026, a dishwasher below about 44 dB(A) is quiet, and below 40 dB(A) very quiet; washing machines below about 72–74 dB(A) during spin are on the quiet side.

short: How much electricity a device uses while running (watts) and over time (kilowatt-hours), which is what you pay for.
body: Watts (W) show the power drawn at a given moment; kilowatt-hours (kWh) measure energy over time. A 100 W TV used for 10 hours uses 1 kWh.
To estimate cost, multiply kWh by your electricity price. For example, a TV using 80 W for 5 hours a day uses about 146 kWh per year; at €0.25 per kWh, that is roughly €37.

Typical power figures on EU labels assume standard settings. Higher brightness, HDR and large screen sizes increase consumption, while eco modes and auto brightness reduce it. Standby use is usually under 0.5 W.
good: In 2026, a 140 cm (55 in) 4K TV typically uses about 60–120 W in SDR; a 68 cm (27 in) monitor usually 15–35 W.
